Jesus Movement
JEE-zus MOOV-ment
proper noun (a 20th-century revival)
The name given to the revival among the youth and counterculture of the late 1960s and 1970s, whose converts were nicknamed “Jesus People” or, derisively, “Jesus freaks.”

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

📖 Biblical Definition

The Jesus Movement was a revival that spread among the youth and counterculture of the late 1960s and 1970s, chiefly in the United States, sweeping many out of the drug culture, the hippie movement, and Eastern mysticism into a professed faith in Jesus Christ. Its converts, nicknamed the “Jesus People,” were marked by zeal, communal living, street evangelism, baptisms in the ocean, and a new style of worship music that became the seedbed of the contemporary worship movement. The dictionary treats the Jesus Movement with discriminating honesty, applying its rule for movements outside the confessional Reformed tradition: honor the genuine work of God, name the weaknesses. Much in it was a true mercy of God. Real conversions occurred; many who had been bound in addiction and despair were savingly changed, owning Jesus as Lord; and a generation that had rejected the establishment church was confronted with the gospel. The Spirit poured out His grace, as He has done in revivals before—and there is no new thing under the sun, for God has often made His people willing in the day of His power. Yet the dictionary also names the real weaknesses that attended it. Much of the movement was doctrinally shallow, suspicious of theology and the institutional church, and easily swept into the charismatic and later word-of-faith excesses; its experiential and anti-creedal instincts left many converts without roots, and not a few of its streams drifted. The dictionary's verdict is the balanced one: the Jesus Movement was a genuine season of grace that gathered a real harvest, weakened by a shallow discipleship and a charismatic enthusiasm that sound doctrine and a confessional church would have guarded. Its abiding lesson is that revival is God's gift, to be received with thanksgiving and shepherded with the Word, lest the harvest be lost for want of rooting.

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The Jesus Movement gathered a real harvest, yet much of it was doctrinally shallow, anti-creedal, and swept into charismatic and word-of-faith excess—a revival weakened for want of sound doctrine and rooted discipleship.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The dictionary applies its rule for movements outside the confessional Reformed tradition: honor the genuine work of God, name the weaknesses. Much in the Jesus Movement was a true mercy. Real conversions occurred; many bound in addiction and despair were savingly changed and owned Jesus as Lord; a generation that had scorned the church was confronted with the gospel. God made His people willing in the day of His power, and the harvest among the young was real. The dictionary will not despise a season in which the Spirit visibly worked.

Yet honesty requires naming the weaknesses. Much of the movement was doctrinally shallow, suspicious of theology, creeds, and the institutional church, and quick to embrace the charismatic enthusiasm and, in some streams, the word-of-faith errors that the dictionary elsewhere rebuts. Its experiential and anti-creedal instincts left many converts without roots, and not a few of its currents drifted into error or burned out. The dictionary's verdict is balanced: a genuine season of grace that gathered a real harvest, weakened by shallow discipleship and a charismatic excess that sound doctrine and a confessional church would have guarded. The abiding lesson is that revival is God's gift, to be received with thanksgiving and shepherded with the Word—for a harvest unrooted is a harvest easily lost.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Named for Jesus, the object of its professed devotion; its converts called the “Jesus People,” a youth-and-counterculture revival of the late 1960s and 1970s.
